videos.script:
Everything you have written so far runs top to bottom, once, the same way every time. {{straight}} Today it stops doing that.

Two ideas, and they are the last two pieces of the language you need before you can write anything real.

{{sometimes}} The first is doing something only sometimes. A condition, and a block that runs when it holds. You have already seen the shape — it is the indentation, which in this language is the syntax rather than a habit.

{{everything}} The second is doing something to everything. A loop. And here is the part people coming from other languages have to unlearn: in Python you do not count. You do not write for i equals zero, i less than length, i plus plus. You say: for each thing in this collection. The collection hands you the things.

{{why}} That is not a style preference. Counting means an index, an index means an off-by-one, and an off-by-one in a loop is the single most common bug in programming. Iterating the thing itself removes the opportunity.

{{enumerate}} When you genuinely need the position — and sometimes you do — there is a built-in for it, and it hands you both. When you need two collections side by side, there is one for that too.

{{comprehension}} And then the comprehension, which is the piece of syntax that makes Python code look like Python. A list built from another list, in one line, with the filter in it. It is not magic and it is not shorter for its own sake: written well it says *what* you are building where a loop says *how*.

{{limit}} It also has a limit, and this lesson names it. A comprehension that does not fit on one line is a loop wearing the wrong clothes.

The same job, three ways, and I will tell you which one I would keep.

{{task}} Here is the task: from a list of prices, take the ones over a hundred and apply a discount.

{{loop}} First as a loop. An empty list, a `for`, an `if`, an `append`. Six lines. Every one of them says how, and the what — discounted prices over a hundred — is something you assemble in your head from reading them.

{{comp}} Now as a comprehension. One line. The expression first, then where it comes from, then the filter. Read it left to right: price times nought point nine, for each price in prices, where price is over a hundred.

{{map}} And the third way, with `map` and `filter`. Also one line, and I am showing it so you recognise it rather than so you write it — it reads inside out, and the lambda is in the way.

{{keep}} I would keep the comprehension. Not because it is shortest — because the first thing it says is what is being built.

{{break}} But watch what happens when the job grows. Add a rule: skip the ones already discounted, and log the ones that were. Now the comprehension needs a second filter and cannot log anything at all, because there is nowhere to put a statement.

{{rule}} That is the line. A comprehension maps and filters. The moment you want to do something else as well, it is a loop again, and going back is not a defeat.

Four things.

{{iterate}} Iterate the thing, not its index. `for item in items`. When you need the position, `enumerate`. When you need two collections together, `zip`. Almost every `range(len(...))` you will ever write is one of those two in disguise.

{{truthy}} `if items:` rather than `if len(items) > 0:`, and remember from lesson 2 that zero is falsy — so when zero is a real value, ask the question you meant.

{{comprehension}} A comprehension when it fits on a line and says what it builds. A loop when it does not. Both are correct and neither is the clever one.

{{mutate}} And the one that bites without a message: do not change a list while you are iterating it. The loop keeps its own position, the list gets shorter underneath it, and it skips items — silently, with no error, producing an answer that is simply wrong.

{{next}} Next lesson is functions: a name for a piece of work, so it happens once and can be tested. It is also where scope gets explained properly, and where the mutable default from lesson 3 comes back.
